source_text: Βασιλείδης δὲ ἐν τῷ εἰκοστῷ τρίτῳ τῶν Ἐξηγητικῶν περὶ τῶν κατὰ τὸ μαρτύριον κολαζομένων αὐταῖς λέξεσι τάδε φησί· φημὶ γάρ τοι, ὁπόσοι ὑποπίπτουσι ταῖς λεγομέναις θλίψεσιν, ἤτοι ἡμαρτηκότες ἐν ἄλλοις λανθάνοντες πταίσμασιν εἰς τοῦτο ἄγονται τὸ ἀγαθόν, χρηστότητι τοῦ περιάγοντος ἄλλα ἐξ ἄλλων ὄντως ἐγκαλούμενοι, ἵνα μὴ ὡς κατάδικοι ἐπὶ κακοῖς ὁμολογουμένοις πάθωσι, μηδὲ λοιδορούμενοι ὡς ὁ μοιχὸς ἢ ὁ φονεύς, ἀλλ’ ὅτι Χριστιανοὶ † πεφυκότες, ὅπερ αὐτοὺς παρηγορήσει μηδὲ πάσχειν δοκεῖν· κἂν μὴ ἡμαρτηκὼς δ’ ὅλως τις ἐπὶ τὸ παθεῖν γένηται, σπάνιον μέν, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ οὗτος κατ’ ἐπιβουλὴν δυνάμεώς τι πείσεται, ἀλλὰ πείσεται ὡς ἔπασχε καὶ τὸ νήπιον τὸ δοκοῦν οὐχ ἡμαρτηκέναι. εἶθ’ ὑποβὰς πάλιν ἐπιφέρει· ὡς οὖν τὸ νήπιον οὐ προημαρτηκὸς ἢ ἐνεργῶς μὲν οὐχ ἡμαρτηκὸς οὐδέν, ἐν ἑαυτῷ τῷ δὲ τὸ ἁμαρτῆσαι ἔχον, ἐπὰν ὑποβληθῇ τῷ παθεῖν, εὐεργετεῖται τε, πολλὰ κερδαῖνον δύσκολα, οὑτωσὶ δὴ κἂν τέλειος μηδὲν ἡμαρτηκὼς ἔργῳ τύχῃ, δέ, ἃν πάθῃ, τοῦτο ἔπαθεν ἐμφερῶς τῷ νηπίῳ· ἔχων μὲν γὰρ ἐν ἑαυτῷ τὸ ἁμαρτητικόν, ἀφορμὴν δὲ πρὸς τὸ ἡμαρτηκέναι μὴ λαβὼν οὐχ ἡμάρτανεν. ὥστ’ οὐκ αὐτῷ τὸ μὴ ἁμαρτῆσαι λογιστέον. ὡς γὰρ ὁ μοιχεῦσαι θέλων μοιχός ἐστι, κἂν τοῦ μοιχεῦσαι μὴ ἐπιτύχῃ, καὶ ὁ ποιῆσαι φόνον θέλων ἀνδροφόνος ἐστί, κἂν μὴ δύνηται φονεῦσαι, οὑτωσὶ δὴ καὶ τὸν ἀναμάρτητον ὃν λέγω ἐὰν ἴδω πάσχοντα, κἂν μηδὲν ᾖ κακὸν πεπραχώς, κακὸν ἐρῶ τῷ θέλειν ἁμαρτάνειν. πάντ’ ἐρῶ γὰρ μᾶλλον ἢ κακὸν τὸ προνοοῦν ἐρῶ. εἶθ’ ὑποβὰς καὶ περὶ τοῦ κυρίου ἄντικρυς ὡς περὶ ἀνθρώπου λέγει· ἐὰν μέντοι παραλιπὼν τούτους ἅπαντας τοὺς λόγους ἔλθῃς ἐπὶ τὸ δυσωπεῖν με διὰ προσώπων τινῶν, εἰ τύχοι, λέγων, ὁ δεῖνα οὖν ἥμαρτεν, ἔπαθεν γὰρ ὁ δεῖνα, ἐὰν μὲν ἐπιτρέπῃς, ἐρῶ, οὐχ ἥμαρτεν μέν, ὅμοιος δὲ ἦν τῷ πάσχοντι νηπίῳ· εἰ μέντοι σφοδρότερον ἐκβιάσαιο τὸν λόγον, ἐρῶ, ἄνθρωπον ὅντιν’ ἂν ὀνομάσῃς ἄνθρωπον εἶναι, δίκαιον δὲ τὸν θεόν. καθαρὸς γὰρ οὐδείς, ὥσπερ εἶπέ τις, ἀπὸ ῥύπου. ἀλλὰ τῷ Βασιλείδῃ ἡ ὑπόθεσις προαμαρτήσασάν φησι τὴν ψυχὴν ἐν ἑτέρῳ βίῳ τὴν κόλασιν ὑπομένειν ἐνταῦθα, τὴν μὲν ἐκλεκτὴν ἐπιτίμως διὰ μαρτυρίου, τὴν ἄλλην δὲ καθαιρομένην οἰκείᾳ κολάσει.
pass_a_gloss: Basilides says in the twenty-third of the Exegetics concerning the words punishing those according to the testimony, for I say, as many as fall under the so-called afflictions, either having sinned in other hidden faults are led to this good, being truly accused of other things from other things by the kindness of the One leading, so that they may not suffer as condemned for admitted evils, nor be reviled as the adulterer or the murderer, but because they have been made Christians, which will comfort them so as not to seem to suffer; and even if someone has not sinned at all comes to suffer, rare though it is, yet this one will not suffer by force of power, but will suffer as the infant who seems not to have sinned; then adding again he says, so the infant not having sinned beforehand or not being sinful in action, yet having in itself the ability to sin, when subjected to suffering is benefited, gaining much from difficult things, thus even the perfect one not having sinned in deed, if he suffers, has suffered similarly to the infant; for he has in himself the sinful tendency, but having not taken the opportunity to sin, has not sinned; thus the not sinning is not to be reckoned to him; for just as the one wanting to commit adultery is an adulterer, even if he does not attain the act of adultery, and the one wanting to commit murder is a murderer, even if he cannot kill, thus also the one without sin, if I see him suffering, even if he has done no evil, I will say the evil is in the willingness to sin; for I will say all rather than evil is in the forethought; then adding and speaking plainly about the Lord as about a man, if leaving all these words you come to calumniating me through certain persons, if it happens, saying, so-and-so sinned, for so-and-so suffered, if you permit, I will say, he did not sin, but was similar to the suffering infant; if however you force the argument more strongly, I will say, whoever you name a man is a man, and God is just; for no one is pure, as someone said, from filth; but Basilides' hypothesis says the soul having sinned beforehand in another life suffers punishment here, the elect one enduring it through martyrdom, the other being purified by its own punishment.
pass_b_english: In the twenty-third book of his *Exegetics*, Basilides comments on the words that punish people 'according to the testimony.' He says: 'I tell you this: as many as fall under these so-called afflictions, either they have sinned in other hidden faults and are led to this good by the kindness of the One who guides all things, being truly accused of different sins than the ones they are punished for, so that they may not suffer as condemned for admitted evils, nor be reviled as the adulterer or the murderer, but because they have been made Christians— which will comfort them so that they do not even seem to suffer; or even if someone has not sinned at all and comes to suffer (rare though that is), yet this one will not suffer by the force of any power, but will suffer as the infant who seems not to have sinned.'

Then, returning to the point, he adds: 'So the infant, not having sinned beforehand, or at least not having sinned in action, yet having within itself the capacity to sin, when subjected to suffering is benefited, gaining much that is hard to win. Thus even the perfect person who has not sinned in deed, if he suffers, has suffered in a way exactly resembling the infant. For he has within himself the sinful tendency, but because he did not take the opportunity to sin, he did not sin. Therefore the fact that he did not sin is not to be reckoned to his credit. For just as the one who wants to commit adultery is an adulterer, even if he does not accomplish the act, and the one who wants to commit murder is a murderer, even if he cannot kill, so also the sinless one of whom I speak, if I see him suffering, even if he has done no evil, I will say the evil lies in his willingness to sin. For I will say all things rather than say that evil lies in God’s forethought.'

Then, pressing further, he speaks plainly about the Lord as if about a man: ‘If, leaving aside all these arguments, you come to calumniate me through certain persons, saying, “So-and-so sinned, for so-and-so suffered,” then if you permit, I will say: he did not sin, but was like the suffering infant. But if you force the argument more strongly, I will say: whoever you name as a man is a man, and God is just. For no one is pure from filth, as someone has said. But Basilides’ hypothesis says that the soul, having sinned beforehand in another life, endures its punishment here: the elect one enduring it through martyrdom, the other being purified by its own punishment.'

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex conditional and causal structures of the Greek text. Pass A provides a literal rendering, while Pass B provides a fluent, readable version that maintains the nuances of Basilides' argument regarding the 'infant' and the 'willingness to sin'. All clauses, including the distinction between the elect and the non-elect in the final sentence, are preserved.
